en: After nearly 48 years of distinguished service in the legal profession and Judiciary, the career of Hon. Justice Oyebisi Omoleye, JCA, reached a fitting climax last Tuesday, as the Ekiti State Government announced that the new High Court Complex under construction in the State would be named after the retiring Presiding Justice of the Court of Appeal, Ekiti Division, Justice Omoleye. The announcement by Governor Biodun Oyebanji came at a valedictory court session organised in honour of the Jurist, who bowed out of active judicial service on attaining the mandatory retirement age of 70. In addition to immortalising her name, the Governor presented Justice Omoleye with a mini bus ,and disclosed that she would return to officially commission the court complex upon its completion. The ceremony, held at the Court of Appeal, Ado-Ekiti, drew serving and retired judicial officers, Senior Advocates of Nigeria (SANs), government officials, family members and members of the legal profession in celebration of a woman widely acknowledged for her contributions to Nigeria’s justice system. A special Police March parade was also staged in her honour, symbolising the nation’s appreciation for her decades of service to justice and public administration. Paying tribute on behalf of the President of the Court of Appeal, Hon. Justice Monica Dongban-Mensem, CFR, Justice Ali Gumel of the Kano Division described Justice Omoleye as a distinguished Jurist whose career had enriched Nigeria’s jurisprudence, and strengthened the administration of justice. He recalled that she was called to the Nigerian Bar in July 1978, and began her legal career at the Ondo State Ministry of Justice in Akure, where she rose through the ranks to become Director of Public Prosecutions. Her career later took her to the Ekiti State House of Assembly, where she served as Clerk and Director-General, before her appointment to the High Court Bench in 1998. She became the Chief Judge of Ekiti State in 2003, and was elevated to the Court of Appeal in June 2006, eventually becoming Presiding Justice of the appellate court in September 2013. Justice Dongban-Mensem commended her unwavering commitment to justice, noting that she brought integrity, wisdom and exceptional legal knowledge to every division of the Court of Appeal where she served. In an emotional valedictory address, Justice Omoleye reflected on her journey from Ikole-Ekiti to one of the highest judicial offices in the country, saying the Bench had taught her that judicial office was a sacred trust and never a personal possession. According to her, Judges are merely custodians of institutions that existed long before them, and will continue long after they leave office. She also spoke candidly about one of the darkest moments of her life – the death of her husband in 1990, when she was just 34 years old. Justice Omoleye said the painful experience left her with the responsibility of raising her children alone, while pursuing an increasingly demanding judicial career. The retired Jurist urged members of the Bench to uphold fairness, restraint, humility and integrity in the discharge of their constitutional responsibilities. She expressed gratitude to God, her colleagues, members of the Bar, judicial staff, family and friends for standing by her throughout her career. Ekiti State Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice, Mr Dayo Apata, described Justice Omoleye as an accomplished Jurist whose professional life was defined by diligence, courage, discipline and excellence. The federal government has reported the delivery of more than 240 urban renewal and slum-upgrading projects nationwide, with over 100 others at various stages of implementation, as it intensifies efforts to tackle Nigeria’s housing crisis and regenerate deteriorating cities. The minister of Housing and Urban Development, Muttaqha Rabe Darma, disclosed this on Monday in Abuja at the combined commemoration of the 2026 World Habitat Day and World Cities Day, held under the global observance of Urban October. Darma said the government was implementing reforms to expand access to decent and affordable housing, improve urban infrastructure and promote sustainable human settlements under President Bola Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda. He explained that the reforms included strengthening housing institutions, improving land administration, promoting physical planning and establishing local building-materials manufacturing hubs to reduce construction costs, stimulate domestic production and create employment. The minister said the Renewed Hope Cities and Estates Programme was targeting 100,000 housing units across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, with projects in Abuja, Lagos, Kano and other states. He cited the groundbreaking of the 250-unit Renewed Hope Civil Service Estate at Dukpa, Gwagwalada, in August as part of the government’s homeownership drive. However, he acknowledged that high interest rates, limited long-term funding, stringent eligibility requirements and low mortgage penetration remained major obstacles to homeownership. He said the ministry was strengthening housing finance institutions, promoting rent-to-own arrangements and public-private partnerships, and advancing the National Urban Development Policy and other planning frameworks. Darma also called for stronger enforcement of building standards, including the modernisation of the National Building Code, and the development of a reliable National Housing Data Bank to guide investment and policy decisions. The Chief Technical Adviser and Head of the UN-Habitat Nigeria Country Office, Niina Rinne, said Nigeria must look beyond constructing houses to planning better neighbourhoods and cities. Rinne warned that poorly located housing could increase transportation costs, strain infrastructure and expose communities to environmental risks, stressing the need for integrated urban planning, effective land management and clear land-tenure arrangements. She said existing neighbourhoods and informal settlements should also benefit from improved drainage, safer streets, public spaces and climate-resilient infrastructure, adding that communities must participate in decisions affecting their homes and livelihoods. The Managing Director and Chief Executive of the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria, Shehu Usman Osidi, said the bank financed 6,911 affordable housing units in 2025, representing 96 per cent of its annual target of 7,200 units. Osidi disclosed that more than N208 billion in housing and mortgage loans was approved during the period, with over N120 billion disbursed to support housing construction, mortgage financing, home renovation, cooperative housing and rent-to-own initiatives. He said the bank would commence implementation of its non-interest mortgage product and rent assistance scheme before the end of October, adding that the initiatives were designed to expand housing finance options and ease the burden of rent payments for federal civil servants. Osidi also highlighted the National Housing Fund Diaspora Mortgage Loan, which enables Nigerians living abroad to invest in housing back home, saying the bank would continue working with the ministry and other stakeholders to make homeownership more accessible. Rapper Sarkodie has stated that Nigerian artists receive substantial financial support from billionaires and business executives in the country, unlike their Ghanaian counterparts. In a recent episode of the When We Sit podcast, the Azonto crooner said Ghanaian artists often make music on their own, without any financial assistance from fellow Ghanaians. He said Nigerian businessmen love to support and invest in talent, giving Nigerian artists a financial advantage in Africa. "What Ghanaian artists do is organic. I give a business plan; even with that, it is hard to get some people to come in. But in Nigeria, I think they take a lot of risks; most rich people take a lot of risks to put their people on. If I break down what it takes to do the O2 Arena, you will freak out, but then we still have to do it," he said. He recalled meeting Nigerian billionaire Tony Elumelu and being shocked by the amount he told him he was investing in a Nigerian artist, whom he believes is the future of Afrobeats. Sarkodie urged Ghanaian business executives and rich folks to emulate Nigerian business leaders by financially supporting their artists

The Nigerian stock market began the new week on a downward momemtum, as investors profit-taking in Dangote Cement Plc and 38 ithers dragged market capitalization below the N160 trillion mark. The Nigerian Exchange Limited All-Share Index (NGX ASI) declined by 2,261.39 basis or 0.91 per cent to close at 245,278.34 basis points. Consequently, equity market capitalisation fell by N1.47 trillion to close at N159.257 trillion. Market sentiment remained bearish, with 39 decliners, outweighing 15 advancers. Multi Trex Integrated Foods emerged the highest price gainer of 10 per cent to close at 66 kobo, per share. Critical Minerals Financing Corporation (CMFC) followed with a gain of 9.97 per cent to close at N3.64, while Austin Laz & Company advanced by 9.93 per cent to close at N3.21, per share. Thomas Wyatt Nigeria increased by 9.92 per cent to close at N2.66, while Neimeth International Pharmaceuticals added 5.88 per cent to close at N8.10, per share. On the other side, Vitafoam Nigeria led others on the losers’ chart with10 per cent to close at N174.60, per share. Cutix followed with a decline of 9.79 per cent to close at N2.12, while Omatek Venture shed 9.38 per cent to close at N1.45, per share. International Energy Insurance declined by 6.48 per cent to close at N2.02, while Linkage Assurance declined by 6.29 per cent to close at N1.64, per share. The total volume traded advanced by 35.5 per cent to 349.34 million units, valued at N17.99 billion, and exchanged in 43,115 deals. Transactions in the shares of Access Holdings led the activity with 23.439 million shares worth N658.348 million. Livestock Feeds followed with account of 23.143 million shares valued at N403.202 million, while United Bank for Africa (UBA) traded 22.818 million shares valued at N959.123 million. Honeywell Flour Mills traded 22.238 million shares worth N393.646 million, while GTCO traded 14.433 million shares worth N1.777 billion. Analysts noted that the session was characterized by bearish sentiment and stronger trading activity, as increased market participation failed to offset sustained selling pressure. Looking ahead, Cowry Assets Management Limited stated that bargain-hunting could support a near-term recovery, although persistent profit-taking may constrain market gains. The Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Oil), Senator Heineken Lokpobiri, regulators, international and indigenous operators will converge next month to deliberate on how Nigeria can increase oil and gas production and unlock more reserves. The conference is organised by the Nigerian Association of Petroleum Explorationists (NAPE) at its 44th Annual International Conference and Exhibition, scheduled for November 8 to 12, 2026, in Lagos. It is themed: “Unlocking More Barrels: Driving Reserves Growth through Exploration, Local Capabilities and Adaptive Technologies.” President of NAPE, Mrs Olajumoke Ajayi, announced the programme at a press conference in Lagos, saying this year’s edition comes at a critical juncture as Nigeria seeks to increase hydrocarbon reserves and production, strengthen energy security, attract new investments and maximise value from its petroleum resources. Ajayi said the theme was built around three interconnected priorities that must align to deliver growth. She said Nigeria has substantial hydrocarbon potential, but translating potential into reserves requires renewed exploration beyond existing discoveries, deployment of appropriate technologies and an operating environment that attracts and retains capital. The Ministry of Food and Agriculture has announced that Japan Motors Trading Company Limited has donated five branded motorcycles towards the 42nd National Farmers’ Day celebration. In a press release issued on Monday, October 19, 2026, the Ministry said the donation qualified the company as a silver sponsor of the annual event, which recognises the contributions of farmers and fishers to Ghana’s development. “The Ministry remains deeply grateful to the Company for its dedicated commitment to support the celebration and the promotion of agricultural development in Ghana,” the statement, signed by the Ministry’s Public Relations Unit, said

A governorship aspirant on the platform of Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in Ogun State, Topa Olusegun Peter, has threatened to sue the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) over alleged exclusion of his name from the final list. Peter, through his lawyers, Neplus Ultra Attorneys, also asked the commission to verify his nomination records and publish his name as the PDP candidate if its records confirm that he was duly nominated. The recent action of the Commission to enforce the Supreme Court judgement on Electoral Act has equally generated a lot of actions and reactions from some political parties. Reacting in a letter dated October 14, 2026, and addressed to the INEC chairman in Abuja, a copy of which was sighted by Daily Trust on Monday, Peter said there is no lawful basis for his exclusion. The lawyers argued on his behalf that INEC’s final list of candidates, published on October 10, did not contain Peter’s name, claiming he is the party’s duly nominated candidate saying Peter obtained the party’s expression of interest and nomination forms on May 12, 2026, and participated in its governorship primary held on May 27. The lawyers further claimed that the PDP forwarded his nomination particulars to INEC and that his name appeared as entry number 15,783 on the party’s membership register submitted to the commission. They said the client had not been given written reasons for the omission or notified of any objection that could explain the decision. The lawyers asked INEC to complete its verification within 48 hours of receiving the letter, correct the published list where the records establish Peter’s nomination and eligibility, and communicate the outcome of its review in writing. Death is a fact of life, no living thing exists forever, not even nature itself, for it is written that even the best and the brightest, shall pass to the Great Beyond, to become one with Nature and the Grand Architect, to be remembered on this side of the Divide, thereafter by their deeds. And so here we are, in the past few days, in the communications and ideas community, mourning the passing of Patrick Dele Cole, known variously as P.D. Cole, or PDC, 1940 -2026, who died in London on October 17, 2026, at the ripe age of 86. He was a historian, administrator, newspaper columnist, an author, politician, a manager of resources, and one of the most outstanding figures in contemporary Nigerian journalism who lived a life of impact and influence and has now left behind a legacy and a leverage that shine luminously upon him beyond his own humble beginnings. His death coincides perhaps by accident with two other moments of remembrance in our industry: the death recently of Professor Idowu Sobowale on October 8, a retired Professor of Mass Communications at the University of Lagos, who along with other distinguished scholars at the University of Lagos, including Professor Alfred Opubor, Professor Frank Ugboaja, Professor Onuora Nwuneli, Dr. Dele Ogunade, Professor Olatunji Dare, and Professor Ralph Akinfeleye, over the years trained generations of journalism and public relations practitioners in Nigeria. PD Cole also passed away two days to the 40th anniversary of the mysterious death of Dele Giwa, whose writings were celebrated yesterday in Lagos with the publication of a collection of his writings titled “Dele Giwa’s Granite Journalism”, edited by Mr. Ray Ekpu, another icon of the profession, the last surviving member of the famous quartet that established the Newswatch magazine. Dr. Patrick Dele Cole stood at the intersection between scholarship, journalism practice, and public intellectualism, and accordingly, some of the most important developments in Nigerian journalism for over three decades had his fingerprints directly or in the shadows, either by direct participation or by proxy or association. He was associated with both The Daily Times (1975 – 1979) and The Guardian Newspapers (from 1983 – 2026), two major organizations that formed the tap roots for much of everything else in the Nigerian media system. Dr. Dele Cole will be remembered for the quality of his associations, his deep commitment to the institutions he served, and his contributions to deepening that essential interface between media, business, society and public service. I met him at The Guardian Newspapers where I practised journalism for over 21 years serving as member, editorial board and columnist, editorialist, essayist, deputy editorial page editor, deputy editorial board chairman, and eventually as Editorial Page Editor/ Chairman, Editorial Board. Dr. Cole was one of the father figures at The Guardian and a towering presence. He was a friend of the publisher, Mr. Alex Uruemu Ibru and a consultant to The Guardian Editorial Board in which capacity he was a regular presence and contributor to the newspaper’s editorial choices. When Mr. Ibru chose to set up a newspaper company in 1982, he had sought the advice of two of his friends – Chief Olusegun Osoba, a seasoned journalist, who had been editor of The Daily Times , and General Manager of The Herald Newspaper and Dr. Dele Cole, former Managing Director of The Daily Times who had also served in Nigeria’s Cabinet Office. Ibru had been advised by his elder brother, the wealthy and influential Chief Michael Ibru not to venture into a business that will throw him into conflict with authority and the firing range of Nigeria’s intolerant military government, but Ibru was motivated by the passion to publish a newspaper that would give voice to the downtrodden and the voiceless people of Nigeria. Osoba and P.D Cole encouraged him, and thus, The Guardian was born. Mr. Ibru had the resources to fulfil his dream.

The Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of the Rural Electrification Agency, REA, Dr. Abba Aliyu, has cautioned that the Electricity Act (Amendment) Bill, 2025, which seeks to establish the National Authority for Renewable Energy, NARE, constitutes serious risks to Nigeria’s electricity market. In an article on Monday made available to Daily Trust, Aliyu said the Bill currently before the National Assembly would create regulatory confusion and scare investors away from the sector. According to him, the bill which also seeks to transfer renewable-energy functions from NERC, REA and the Rural Electrification Fund to a new authority, and allocate 40 percent of the Rural Electrification Fund to it, will cause fragmentation to a market with a viable market. Sixteen states, he said, have already received regulatory oversight from NERC under the Electricity Act 2023, stressing that bringing another federal regulator organised around technology will create a new axis of jurisdiction. He said: “We could end up with NERC, State commissions, NARE, NEMSA and other institutions interacting with different aspects of the same project. That is not simplification. It is fragmentation.” He hinted that Nigeria’s distributed-energy market is beginning to show results, with over 1,000 mini-grids under development and $750 million DARES programme targeting 17.5 million Nigerians, 1,225 mini-grids and 465MW. He announced that REA has secured N350 billion potential domestic financing commitments – FCMB N100bn, Lotus Bank N100bn, Alpha Morgan N50bn and Stanbic IBTC N100bn. Aliyu maintained that investors need predictable rules for 15 to 20-year investments, warning that ambiguity increases cost of capital and e tariffs. He added that diverting the Rural Electrification Fund to fund a new institution confuses instrument with objective, stressing that every naira should be judged by how many Nigerians it connects. The National Assembly, he advised, should conduct regulatory-impact analysis and get feedback from states, investors and development partners before taking a decision. Investigative journalist Manasseh Azure Awuni has challenged reports that the Ashanti Regional office of the Ghana Education Service (GES) has exonerated the headmaster of Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS), Zakaria Abdulai, over allegations of sexual abuse involving female students. He has questioned the regional education authorities’ capacity to determine allegations involving rape, arguing that the matter requires a criminal investigation by the police. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Monday, October 19, Mr Azure said any claim that the headmaster had been cleared by the regional office was deeply troubling, particularly given reports that complaints had previously been made to school authorities. “I think it's the biggest insult to the victims and Ghanaians to say that the GES exonerated him,” he said. “This GES is within the enclave. These are the people who should have acted when reports upon reports went out." The journalist said the committee that reportedly examined the matter was chaired by the Obuasi East Director of Education, raising questions about the process and its ability to address allegations of a criminal nature. He also referred to concerns he said had been expressed by people in the Obuasi area about the response of school management and regional education authorities to the alleged incidents. “Obuasi East and Obuasi West are so close. And if you go to that enclave, there are people who say that from the school's management to the regional GES looked away when these things happened,” he said. Mr Azure questioned whether the committee had the expertise and mandate to investigate allegations of rape, insisting that such claims should be handled through the criminal justice system. “So if those same people come out to say they have cleared him, they have exonerated him, these are allegations of rape,” he said. “Which of them on that committee is equipped to investigate rape? This is a police, a criminal matter.” The allegations are the subject of Manasseh Azure Awuni’s documentary, Inside the Dreaded Headmaster’s Bungalow . It examines alleged sexual abuse involving female students at Obuasi Senior High Technical School. Mr Azure’s comments come amid public concern over reports that female students had made allegations of rape, sexual harassment, sexual assault and other forms of abuse involving the headmaster. The allegations, which have attracted attention following the report by Mr Azure, have also prompted calls for the affected students to be protected from intimidation and for their complaints to be investigated independently. A GES administrative inquiry and a police criminal investigation serve different purposes. Any determination of criminal responsibility must follow the applicable legal process. The claims against Mr Abdulai remain allegations and must be established through a fair and credible investigation. The matter has raised broader questions about how schools handle complaints of sexual abuse, the protection available to students who report alleged misconduct and the accountability of education authorities when concerns are brought to their attention
